title: Human Body and Health: Body Systems, Homeostasis, Nutrition, and Disease
objectives: Students will identify the major human body systems, name their main organs and jobs, and explain how two or more systems work together.
Students will explain homeostasis and trace a feedback loop (stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, response), telling negative feedback from positive feedback.
Students will read a Nutrition Facts label and calculate Calories from carbohydrate, protein, and fat (4, 4, and 9 Calories per gram).
Students will classify diseases as infectious or noninfectious, compare types of pathogens, and explain how the immune system and vaccines provide protection.
Students will interpret health data in tables and graphs (such as heart-rate and disease-rate tables) and choose conclusions the data support.
teach:
Week 4 Science: Human Body and Health — Body Systems, Homeostasis, Nutrition, and Disease

Objectives

  • Identify the major body systems, their main organs, and their jobs; explain how systems interact.
  • Explain homeostasis and trace a feedback loop; tell negative feedback from positive feedback.
  • Read a Nutrition Facts label and calculate Calories from carbohydrate, protein, and fat.
  • Classify diseases as infectious or noninfectious; compare bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites; explain immunity and vaccines.
  • Interpret heart-rate tables, nutrition labels, and disease-rate tables, and choose conclusions the data support.

Teacher note: Keep all health content factual and general. If a student asks about a personal health concern, acknowledge the question and suggest they talk with a doctor or other health professional. This lesson teaches how the body works and how to read health data; it does not give personal medical or diet advice.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors.
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • A real food package with a Nutrition Facts label, or the sample label in the guided practice.
  • A watch or phone with a seconds display (for the warm-up pulse count).
  • Calculator.
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Pulse count and "What changes when you climb stairs?" Connect each change to a body system.
Direct instruction20Body systems; homeostasis and feedback loops; nutrition and Calories; pathogens and immunity; Worked Examples 1–3.
Guided practice15Read a real or sample nutrition label and a heart-rate table with teacher support.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket, study plan, and this week's Practice GED.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Have students find their pulse at the wrist or neck, count beats for 15 seconds, and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute (bpm). Then ask: "Imagine you just ran up three flights of stairs. Name three things that change in your body." Write answers on the board and ask which body system is responsible for each.

Expected answers:

  • Heart beats faster and harder → circulatory system (moves more blood, oxygen, and nutrients to muscles).
  • Breathing gets faster and deeper → respiratory system (takes in more oxygen, removes more carbon dioxide).
  • Sweating, face turns red → integumentary system (skin) helping cool the body; the nervous system triggers it.
  • Leg muscles burn or feel tired → muscular system working hard and using energy.

Point to make: No system works alone; the nervous system coordinates them. Pulse check: 18 beats in 15 seconds is 18 × 4 = 72 bpm.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Levels of organization (2 minutes). Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Example: muscle cells form muscle tissue; muscle tissue (plus other tissues) forms the heart; the heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system.

2. The major body systems (5 minutes). Put this table on the board. Students do not need every detail, but they must match each system to its job.

SystemMain organsMain job
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels, bloodTransports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and wastes
RespiratoryNose, trachea, lungsTakes in oxygen; removes carbon dioxide
DigestiveMouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreasBreaks food into nutrients and absorbs them
Excretory (urinary)Kidneys, bladderFilters blood; removes liquid waste; balances water
NervousBrain, spinal cord, nervesSenses changes, sends signals, controls responses
EndocrineGlands such as the pancreas, thyroid, adrenal glandsReleases hormones (chemical messengers) into the blood
Muscular and skeletalMuscles, bones, jointsMovement, support, protection
Immune (with lymphatic)White blood cells, lymph nodes, spleenDefends against pathogens
IntegumentarySkin, hair, nailsBarrier against germs; helps control temperature

Teamwork examples: the lungs load oxygen into the blood and the heart pumps it to every cell; the small intestine absorbs nutrients into the blood, which carries them to cells.

3. Homeostasis and feedback (5 minutes). Homeostasis is keeping the body's internal conditions stable even when the outside world changes. Examples: body temperature near 37 °C (98.6 °F), blood glucose (sugar) in a normal range, water balance. The body uses feedback loops:

Stimulus (a change) → Receptor/sensor (detects it) → Control center (often the brain; compares to the normal set point) → Effector (a muscle or gland that acts) → Response (the change is reversed or increased)

  • Negative feedback reverses a change and brings conditions back toward normal. It is how most homeostasis works. Too hot → sweat and widen skin blood vessels → body cools. Too cold → shiver and narrow skin blood vessels → body warms. Blood glucose high after a meal → pancreas releases insulin → cells take in glucose → blood glucose falls. Blood glucose low → pancreas releases glucagon → liver releases stored glucose → blood glucose rises.
  • Positive feedback increases a change until an event ends it. Childbirth: contractions trigger release of the hormone oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions, until the baby is born. Clotting: platelets at a cut attract more platelets until the cut is sealed.

Memory aid: Negative = "No, go back." Positive = "More, more, more."

4. Nutrition and energy (4 minutes). Food supplies energy and building materials. The energy in food is measured in Calories (a food Calorie with a capital C is a kilocalorie, or 1,000 small calories). Three macronutrients supply energy:

Carbohydrate: 4 Calories per gram  |  Protein: 4 Calories per gram  |  Fat: 9 Calories per gram

Vitamins, minerals, water, and fiber do not supply Calories but are still needed. On a Nutrition Facts label, every number is for one serving; if a person eats two servings, double everything. The % Daily Value (%DV) is based on a general 2,000-Calorie daily diet; as a guide, 5% DV or less is low and 20% DV or more is high. Energy balance: if a person takes in more Calories than the body uses over time, the extra is stored (mostly as fat); if the person uses more than he or she takes in, stored energy is used.

5. Disease, pathogens, and immunity (4 minutes).

  • Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (germs) and spread between people. Noninfectious diseases cannot be caught; they are linked to genes, lifestyle, environment, or aging (type 2 diabetes, most heart disease).
  • Bacteria: living single cells (strep throat); antibiotics can kill them. Viruses: not cells; reproduce only inside host cells (cold, flu, measles). Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and overusing them helps bacteria develop antibiotic resistance. Fungi: athlete's foot. Parasites: protists such as the malaria parasite, and parasitic worms.
  • How pathogens spread: droplets in the air, direct contact, contaminated food or water, and vectors (animals such as mosquitoes and ticks that carry pathogens).
  • Lines of defense: (1) Barriers: skin, mucus, stomach acid. (2) General: inflammation, fever, white blood cells that engulf invaders. (3) Targeted: white blood cells make antibodies that attach to one specific pathogen, and memory cells remain so the body responds faster next time. That is immunity.
  • Vaccines expose the immune system to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen, so the body makes memory cells without having the disease. When most people are immune, a pathogen has trouble spreading, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated (community immunity).

Worked Example 1 — Trace a feedback loop

Scenario: Two hours after lunch, Dana's blood glucose is higher than normal. Cells in her pancreas detect the rise and release insulin into the blood. Insulin signals muscle, liver, and fat cells to take in glucose. Dana's blood glucose falls back into the normal range, and the pancreas releases less insulin.

Solution:

  • Stimulus: blood glucose rises above normal.
  • Receptor and control center: cells in the pancreas (in this loop, the pancreas both detects the change and decides how much insulin to release).
  • Messenger: insulin, a hormone, so this loop involves the endocrine system; the circulatory system carries the insulin.
  • Effectors: muscle, liver, and fat cells take in glucose.
  • Response: blood glucose falls back toward normal.
  • Type: negative feedback, because the response reverses the original change (high goes back down). Once glucose is normal, the signal (insulin release) decreases, which "shuts off" the loop.

Worked Example 2 — Calories on a nutrition label

Label (sample yogurt): Serving size 1 cup (227 g); Servings per container 2; Calories 150; Total fat 2 g; Total carbohydrate 20 g; Protein 13 g.

Questions and solutions:

  1. Calories from each macronutrient in one serving:
    Fat: 2 g × 9 = 18 Calories
    Carbohydrate: 20 g × 4 = 80 Calories
    Protein: 13 g × 4 = 52 Calories
    Check: 18 + 80 + 52 = 150 Calories, which matches the label.
  2. Percent of Calories from protein: 52 ÷ 150 = 0.3466… ≈ 35%.
  3. A person eats the whole container. Servings eaten = 2, so Calories = 2 × 150 = 300 Calories, and protein = 2 × 13 g = 26 g.

Teaching point: The most common GED trap is forgetting servings per container. Have students circle "Servings per container" on every label before reading anything else.

Worked Example 3 — Read a heart-rate table

Data: One person's heart rate during and after a 6-minute walk on a treadmill.

TimeHeart rate (bpm)
Before walking (rest)70
End of minute 298
End of minute 4112
End of minute 6116
2 minutes after stopping84

Questions and solutions:

  1. Increase from rest to the end of minute 6: 116 − 70 = 46 bpm.
  2. Percent increase: 46 ÷ 70 = 0.657… ≈ 66%.
  3. Pattern: heart rate rose quickly at first (+28 in the first 2 minutes), then more slowly (+14, then +4), and dropped after the walk.
  4. Explanation: working muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, so the heart pumps faster; after exercise, negative feedback brings heart rate back toward its resting level.
  5. Limit: this is one person on one day, so we cannot generalize these exact numbers to everyone.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Part A — Label. Use a real package or this sample: Serving size 3 crackers (30 g); Servings per container 8; Calories 140; Total fat 5 g; Total carbohydrate 21 g; Protein 2 g; Sodium 230 mg (10% DV).

  1. How many Calories come from fat in one serving?
  2. Show that the label's Calorie total is about right.
  3. A person eats 9 crackers. How many servings is that, and how many Calories?
  4. Is this food low, moderate, or high in sodium based on %DV?
  1. 5 g × 9 = 45 Calories.
  2. Fat 45 + carbohydrate (21 × 4 = 84) + protein (2 × 4 = 8) = 137 Calories. Labels round, so 137 ≈ 140.
  3. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 servings; 3 × 140 = 420 Calories.
  4. Moderate: 10% is between 5% (low) and 20% (high).

Part B — Feedback. Read aloud: "A person walks outside on a freezing day. Nerve endings in the skin detect the cold. The brain sends signals to skeletal muscles, which begin to shiver. Shivering produces heat, and body temperature stays near normal."

  1. Name the stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, and response.
  2. Is this negative or positive feedback? How do you know?
  1. Stimulus: cold / body temperature starting to drop. Receptor: nerve endings in the skin. Control center: the brain (specifically the hypothalamus). Effector: skeletal muscles. Response: shivering produces heat.
  2. Negative feedback: the response (warming) reverses the change (cooling).

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–12 on the course page while you circulate. Unfinished items become homework.

Checks for Understanding (use during the wrap-up)

  • "Which system carries oxygen to the muscles?" Expected: the circulatory system (the respiratory system brings oxygen into the blood first).
  • "Sweating on a hot day: negative or positive feedback?" Expected: negative, because it reverses the rise in temperature.
  • "How many Calories in 10 grams of fat?" Expected: 10 × 9 = 90 Calories.
  • "Will an antibiotic cure the flu?" Expected: no; flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics work only against bacteria.
  • "How does a vaccine protect a person?" Expected: it lets the immune system make memory cells without causing the disease, so the body responds quickly if the real pathogen appears.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Thinking "negative feedback" means "bad." Correction: negative means the response goes in the opposite direction of the change. Most negative feedback is healthy and normal.

Forgetting servings per container. Correction: circle "servings per container" first. Multiply every label number by the number of servings actually eaten.

Using 4 Calories per gram for fat. Correction: write "4-4-9" (carbohydrate, protein, fat) at the top of scratch paper before any label question.

Saying antibiotics kill viruses, or confusing antibiotics with antibodies. Correction: antibiotics are medicines that target bacteria only; antibodies are made by the body. Ask, "Is the pathogen a living cell?"

Treating a pattern as proof of cause. In disease-rate tables, two things may change together (correlation) without one being proven to cause the other. Correction: pick the answer that describes what the data show, not one that goes beyond them.

Differentiation

Support: Give students the body-systems table as a reference card and a blank five-box feedback-loop diagram to fill in together. For label math, provide a frame: "___ g fat × 9 = ___; ___ g carbs × 4 = ___; ___ g protein × 4 = ___."

Stretch: Have students explain how three systems interact during a meal (digestive absorbs, circulatory transports, endocrine regulates with insulin). Or have them find the percent of Calories from each macronutrient on a label and check that the percents add to about 100%.

How This Shows Up on the GED

Human body and health is part of life science on the GED Science test. Questions give a short passage, a label, a described diagram, or a data table. Expect wording like:

  • "Which body system is most directly responsible for …?"
  • "Which statement describes a negative feedback mechanism?"
  • "Based on the label, how many Calories would a person consume by eating the entire package?"
  • "Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?"
  • "Which type of pathogen is most likely responsible?" or "Why would an antibiotic be ineffective?"

Formats include multiple choice, drop-down, drag-and-drop (sorting organs into systems), fill-in-the-blank calculations (Calories, a mean, a percent), and hot spots (clicking the sentence or part of a diagram that shows a step). The on-screen calculator is available. Teach this routine for every health data question: (1) read the title, units, and labels; (2) find the exact row or column the question asks about; (3) calculate if needed; (4) choose the answer that the data actually show.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above, then preview the exit ticket, the study plan, and this week's Practice GED.
student:
Human Body and Health

Your body is a team of systems that work together all day to keep you alive and steady. On the GED Science test, you will read about the body, read nutrition labels and health data, and answer questions about how the body stays balanced and how it fights disease. This lesson gives you the key ideas and the math you need.

1. Body systems work as a team

Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems. Here are the systems that show up most often:

SystemMain partsMain job
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels, bloodCarries oxygen, nutrients, and wastes
RespiratoryLungs, tracheaBrings in oxygen; removes carbon dioxide
DigestiveStomach, intestines, liverBreaks down food; absorbs nutrients
ExcretoryKidneys, bladderFilters blood; removes liquid waste
NervousBrain, spinal cord, nervesSenses changes and sends signals
EndocrineGlands (pancreas, thyroid)Sends hormones through the blood
ImmuneWhite blood cells, lymph nodesFights pathogens (germs)
Muscular / skeletalMuscles, bonesMovement and support

Systems depend on each other. When you exercise, your respiratory system takes in more oxygen, your circulatory system pumps it faster to your muscles, and your nervous system coordinates it all.

2. Homeostasis: staying balanced

Homeostasis means keeping conditions inside the body stable, such as body temperature (about 37 °C or 98.6 °F), blood sugar, and water. The body does this with feedback loops:

Stimulus (a change) → Receptor (detects it) → Control center (usually the brain; decides) → Effector (muscle or gland acts) → Response

  • Negative feedback reverses a change and brings the body back to normal. Too hot? You sweat. Blood sugar too high? The pancreas releases insulin, and cells take in sugar. Most homeostasis works this way.
  • Positive feedback makes a change grow stronger until something ends it. Examples: contractions during childbirth, and blood clotting at a cut.

Memory aid: Negative = "No, go back." Positive = "More, more, more."

Worked Example 1 — Feedback loop

On a cold day, nerve endings in Marcus's skin detect the cold. His brain signals his muscles to shiver, which produces heat, and his body temperature stays near normal.

Stimulus: cold. Receptor: nerve endings in the skin. Control center: brain. Effector: muscles. Response: shivering makes heat. Type: negative feedback, because warming reverses the cooling.

3. Nutrition and energy

Food gives your body energy, measured in Calories. Three nutrients supply Calories:

Carbohydrate = 4 Calories per gram
Protein = 4 Calories per gram
Fat = 9 Calories per gram

Vitamins, minerals, fiber, and water have no Calories, but your body still needs them.

Reading a Nutrition Facts label:

  1. Find servings per container and serving size first. Every number on the label is for one serving.
  2. Multiply by the number of servings actually eaten.
  3. The % Daily Value (%DV) shows how much of a day's amount one serving gives, based on a general 2,000-Calorie diet. 5% or less is low; 20% or more is high.

Worked Example 2 — Label math

A cereal label says: Serving size 1 cup; Servings per container 6; Calories 160; Total fat 2 g; Total carbohydrate 33 g; Protein 3 g.

a) Calories from fat in one serving: 2 g × 9 = 18 Calories.

b) Check the total: fat 18 + carbohydrate (33 × 4 = 132) + protein (3 × 4 = 12) = 162 Calories. Labels round, so 162 ≈ 160.

c) Someone eats 2 cups: that is 2 servings, so 2 × 160 = 320 Calories.

Energy balance: If a person takes in more Calories than the body uses over time, the extra energy is stored, mostly as fat. If the person uses more than he or she takes in, the body uses stored energy.

4. Reading heart-rate data

Heart rate is measured in beats per minute (bpm). During exercise, muscles need more oxygen, so heart rate rises. After exercise, negative feedback brings it back toward the resting rate.

Worked Example 3 — Heart-rate table

PersonResting (bpm)After 5 minutes of jumping rope (bpm)
168142
276150
360128

Mean resting heart rate: (68 + 76 + 60) ÷ 3 = 204 ÷ 3 = 68 bpm.

Largest increase: Person 1: 142 − 68 = 74. Person 2: 150 − 76 = 74. Person 3: 128 − 60 = 68. Persons 1 and 2 tied at 74 bpm.

Careful conclusion: In this small group, every person's heart rate rose after jumping rope. Three people are not enough to make claims about everyone.

5. Disease and pathogens

Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (germs) and can spread from person to person. Noninfectious diseases (such as type 2 diabetes and most heart disease) cannot be caught from someone; they are linked to genes, lifestyle, environment, or age.

PathogenWhat it isExamplesAntibiotics work?
BacteriaLiving single cellsStrep throat, some food poisoningYes
VirusNot a cell; reproduces only inside host cellsCommon cold, flu, measlesNo
FungusYeast or mold-like organismsAthlete's foot, ringwormNo (other medicines are used)
ParasiteProtists or worms living on or in a hostMalaria (spread by mosquitoes)No (other medicines are used)

Pathogens spread through the air (droplets from coughs and sneezes), touch, contaminated food or water, and vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks.

6. How the body fights back

  1. Barriers: skin, mucus, tears, and stomach acid keep many germs out.
  2. General defenses: inflammation, fever, and white blood cells that swallow invaders.
  3. Targeted defenses: white blood cells make antibodies that lock onto one specific pathogen. Memory cells stay behind, so the next time the body meets that pathogen, it responds faster. This is immunity.

A vaccine trains the immune system using a harmless form or piece of a pathogen, so the body builds memory cells without getting the disease. When most people in a community are immune, the pathogen has a hard time spreading. This is called community immunity (or herd immunity).

Don't mix these up: antibodies are made by your body. Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria.

Try It

1. Which body system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients into the blood?

Show answer

The digestive system. (The small intestine absorbs nutrients, and the circulatory system then carries them to cells.)

2. When the body becomes dehydrated, the brain signals the kidneys to save water, so less urine is made. Is this negative or positive feedback?

Show answer

Negative feedback. The body is low on water, and the response (saving water) works to reverse that change.

3. One serving of a snack has 7 g of fat, 15 g of carbohydrate, and 4 g of protein. How many Calories is that?

Show answer

Fat: 7 × 9 = 63. Carbohydrate: 15 × 4 = 60. Protein: 4 × 4 = 16. Total: 63 + 60 + 16 = 139 Calories.

4. A label says 2.5 servings per container and 120 Calories per serving. How many Calories are in the whole container?

Show answer

2.5 × 120 = 300 Calories.

5. Why can a person who had chickenpox as a child usually fight off the same virus quickly later in life?

Show answer

The first infection left behind memory cells. When the same virus enters again, these cells quickly trigger antibody production, so the body stops the virus before it causes illness. This is immunity.
post:
Post Lesson: Human Body and Health

Summary of Key Points

  • Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems. Systems work together; for example, the respiratory system brings in oxygen, and the circulatory system delivers it.
  • Homeostasis keeps internal conditions stable. A feedback loop runs stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → response.
  • Negative feedback reverses a change (sweating, shivering, insulin). Positive feedback makes a change stronger until an event ends it (childbirth, clotting).
  • Carbohydrate and protein give 4 Calories per gram; fat gives 9. Every label number is per serving, so multiply by servings eaten.
  • Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.
  • The immune system uses barriers, general defenses, and targeted defenses (antibodies and memory cells). Vaccines build memory cells without causing the disease.
  • When reading health data, describe what the data show; do not claim more than the data support.

Exit Ticket

1. Name the system that sends hormones such as insulin through the body.

Show answer

The endocrine system (the hormones travel in the blood of the circulatory system).

2. A food has 12 g of fat per serving. How many Calories come from fat?

Show answer

12 × 9 = 108 Calories.

3. During childbirth, contractions cause the release of a hormone that causes even stronger contractions. Is this negative or positive feedback?

Show answer

Positive feedback; the response increases the original change until the baby is born.

4. A friend wants antibiotics for a cold. Why will they not help?

Show answer

Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, which reproduce inside the body's own cells.

5. Four people's resting heart rates are 62, 70, 74, and 66 bpm. What is the mean?

Show answer

(62 + 70 + 74 + 66) ÷ 4 = 272 ÷ 4 = 68 bpm.

Reflection

  • Describe something your body did today to keep itself balanced (for example, feeling thirsty, sweating, or shivering). Which feedback loop was working?
  • Which part of this lesson was easiest for you: body systems, feedback, label math, or disease and immunity? Which part needs more practice?
  • Look at the label on a food you eat often. What surprised you about the serving size or the number of servings?

This Week's Study Plan

DayTask (20–40 minutes)
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Make flash cards for the vocabulary terms. Complete the Try It problems without looking at the answers.
Day 2Body systems and feedback: from memory, write the five steps of a feedback loop and one negative and one positive example. Do practice items 1–6.
Day 3Nutrition math: find three Nutrition Facts labels at home and calculate the Calories from fat, carbohydrate, and protein for each. Do practice items 7–12.
Day 4Disease and immunity: make a two-column chart comparing bacteria and viruses. Review any practice items you missed and reread their explanations.
Day 5Take this week's Practice GED in one sitting with the timer on.
Day 6Review every Practice GED question you missed. Write one sentence for each explaining the correct answer. Reread the Study Notes.

Test-Taking Strategy: Read the Units and Labels First

Before answering a question about a nutrition label or a data table, spend a few seconds on the title, the column headings, and the units (grams, Calories, beats per minute, cases per 100,000 people). Many wrong answers on the GED come from using the right method on the wrong number, such as using one serving when the question asks about the whole package. Underline or note the exact row and column the question asks about, then calculate.

vocab.def: A group of organs that work together to do one major job in the body.
vocab.example: The heart, blood vessels, and blood make up the circulatory system.

vocab.def: Keeping the body's internal conditions stable even when outside conditions change.
vocab.example: Body temperature stays near 37 °C on both hot and cold days.

vocab.def: A cycle in which the body detects a change and responds to it: stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, response.
vocab.example: Skin senses heat, the brain signals sweat glands, sweat cools the body.

vocab.def: A response that reverses a change and brings conditions back toward normal.
vocab.example: Insulin lowers blood sugar after it rises following a meal.

vocab.def: A response that makes a change grow stronger until an event ends it.
vocab.example: Contractions during childbirth get stronger until the baby is born.

vocab.def: The muscle or gland that carries out the body's response in a feedback loop.
vocab.example: Sweat glands are effectors when the body is too hot.

vocab.def: A chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to other parts of the body.
vocab.example: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas.

vocab.def: A unit of energy in food (a food Calorie equals one kilocalorie).
vocab.example: One gram of fat supplies 9 Calories.

vocab.def: A nutrient the body needs in large amounts that supplies energy: carbohydrate, protein, or fat.
vocab.example: Bread is mostly carbohydrate; chicken is mostly protein.

vocab.def: A germ that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite.
vocab.example: The flu virus is a pathogen.

vocab.def: A tiny pathogen that is not a cell and can reproduce only inside a host's cells; antibiotics do not kill it.
vocab.example: The common cold is caused by viruses.

vocab.def: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing; it does not work on viruses.
vocab.example: A doctor may prescribe an antibiotic for strep throat, a bacterial infection.

vocab.def: A protein made by white blood cells that attaches to a specific pathogen and helps destroy it.
vocab.example: After a measles infection, the body makes antibodies against the measles virus.

vocab.def: A preparation that trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the disease.
vocab.example: A flu vaccine helps the body build memory cells against flu viruses.

vocab.def: An animal, such as a mosquito or tick, that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

notes:
Study Notes: Human Body and Health

Body Systems

SystemJob
CirculatoryTransports O2, nutrients, wastes
RespiratoryTakes in O2, removes CO2
DigestiveBreaks down and absorbs food
ExcretoryKidneys filter blood; water balance
NervousSenses and signals; control center
EndocrineHormones (insulin, glucagon)
ImmuneFights pathogens
Muscular/skeletalMovement, support
SkinBarrier; cooling by sweat

Feedback Loop

Stimulus → Receptor → Control center → Effector → Response

Negative ("No, go back"): reverses change. Sweating, shivering, insulin lowers high blood sugar, glucagon raises low blood sugar, kidneys save water.
Positive ("More, more"): increases change until an event ends it. Childbirth, blood clotting.

Nutrition Math

4-4-9: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 Calories per gram.

Calories eaten = Calories per serving × servings eaten.

% of Calories from fat = (fat g × 9) ÷ total Calories × 100.

%DV: 5% or less = low; 20% or more = high (2,000-Calorie basis).

Pathogens

Bacteria: living cells; antibiotics work.
Viruses: not cells; need host cells; antibiotics do NOT work.
Fungi, parasites: other medicines.
Spread: air droplets, touch, food/water, vectors (mosquitoes, ticks).

Immunity

1. Barriers (skin, mucus, acid) → 2. General (fever, inflammation, white blood cells) → 3. Targeted (antibodies, memory cells).
Vaccine = memory cells without the disease. Community immunity protects those who are not immune.

Data checklist: title → units → correct row/column → calculate → choose what the data actually show (pattern ≠ proof of cause). Mean: add values, divide by how many. Percent change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100.

stimuli.title: Heart Rate Before and After Exercise
stimuli.html:
A student measured the heart rates of four adult volunteers. Each volunteer first sat quietly for 5 minutes, and the student recorded the resting heart rate. Each volunteer then jogged in place for 4 minutes. The student recorded each heart rate immediately after jogging stopped and again 1, 2, and 3 minutes later while the volunteer sat quietly. items.prompt: During exercise, the lungs take in extra oxygen. Which body system carries that oxygen from the lungs to the working muscles?
items.hint: Which system includes the heart, blood vessels, and blood?
items.explain:
Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs (respiratory system). The circulatory system, made of the heart, blood vessels, and blood, then pumps that oxygen-rich blood to the muscles. This is an example of two systems working together.

The digestive system absorbs nutrients from food, the excretory system filters wastes from the blood, and the endocrine system sends hormones. None of them carries oxygen.

items.prompt: Which volunteer had the lowest resting heart rate?
items.hint: Look only at the Resting column.
items.explain:
Resting heart rates: A = 64, B = 72, C = 58, D = 70 bpm. The lowest is 58 bpm, Volunteer C.

Volunteer A (64) is the second lowest. Volunteer B has the highest resting rate, so choosing B means reading the column backward.

items.prompt: Sort each body part into the organ system it belongs to.
items.hint: Ask what each part does: pumps or carries blood, moves air, handles food, or carries nerve signals.
items.explain:
• Circulatory: heart (pumps blood) and arteries (carry blood away from the heart).
  • Respiratory: lungs (exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide) and trachea (the airway to the lungs).
  • Digestive: small intestine (absorbs nutrients from food).
  • Nervous: spinal cord (carries signals between the brain and the body).

A common mistake is to place the trachea with the digestive system because it is in the throat. The trachea carries air, not food; the esophagus is the food tube.

items.prompt: A person eats the entire package of granola bars. How many Calories does the person consume?
items.hint: Check the servings per container. The Calories listed are for one serving.
items.explain:
The label lists 200 Calories per serving and 2 servings per container.

Calories in the whole package = 200 × 2 = 400 Calories.

200 is the amount for just one bar; it ignores the servings per container. 90 comes from adding the gram weights of both bars (45 + 45), which are grams, not Calories. 100 is half of a serving, not the whole package.

items.prompt: Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram. How many Calories in one serving of the granola bar come from fat?
items.hint: Find the grams of total fat in one serving and multiply by 9.
items.explain:
Total fat in one serving = 8 g.

Calories from fat = 8 g × 9 Calories/g = 72 Calories.

A common error is multiplying by 4 (8 × 4 = 32). The value 4 Calories per gram is for carbohydrate and protein; fat supplies 9. Another error is using the %DV (10%) instead of the grams.

items.prompt: The mean (average) heart rate of the four volunteers was 66 bpm at rest. What was the increase in the mean heart rate from resting to immediately after jogging?
items.hint: First find the mean of the Immediately after jogging column, then subtract the resting mean.
items.explain:
Mean immediately after jogging = (128 + 140 + 116 + 136) ÷ 4 = 520 ÷ 4 = 130 bpm.

Check the resting mean: (64 + 72 + 58 + 70) ÷ 4 = 264 ÷ 4 = 66 bpm.

Increase = 130 − 66 = 64 bpm.

130 bpm is the mean after jogging, not the increase. 82 bpm is the highest value in the table minus the lowest (140 − 58), which mixes different volunteers and different times. 58 bpm is Volunteer C's increase (116 − 58), not the mean increase.

items.prompt: The passage describes how the body responds to rising temperature. Click the sentence that describes the receptor (sensor) step of the feedback loop.
spans: On a hot afternoon, a hiker's body temperature begins to rise above its normal level of about 37 °C.
Temperature-sensing nerve cells in the skin and in the brain detect the change.
The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, compares this information to the body's normal set point and sends out signals.
Sweat glands in the skin respond by releasing sweat.
As the sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the body.
The hiker's body temperature moves back toward normal.
items.hint: The receptor is the part that first notices, or detects, the change.
items.explain:
In a feedback loop, the receptor detects the change. Sentence 2 says temperature-sensing nerve cells "detect the change," so it is the receptor step.

  • Sentence 1 is the stimulus (the change itself).
  • Sentence 3 is the control center (the hypothalamus compares to the set point and sends signals).
  • Sentence 4 describes the effector (sweat glands).
  • Sentences 5 and 6 describe the response and its result.

Students often click sentence 3 because it mentions the brain, but the hypothalamus is acting as the control center, not the sensor.

items.prompt: A student has a cold caused by a virus. A friend offers leftover antibiotics. Which statement best explains why antibiotics would not cure the cold?
options: Antibiotics attack structures and processes found in bacteria, and viruses are not cells and lack those structures.
Antibiotics work only against fungi, and colds are caused by viruses.
Viruses are much larger than bacteria, so antibiotics cannot surround them.
A cold is a noninfectious disease, so medicine cannot affect it.
items.hint: Think about what kind of pathogen antibiotics are designed to kill and whether a virus is a living cell.
items.explain:
Antibiotics target parts and processes of bacterial cells, such as the bacterial cell wall. A virus is not a cell; it reproduces only inside the host's own cells and has none of those bacterial parts, so antibiotics have nothing to attack.

Antibiotics are designed for bacteria, not fungi. Viruses are much smaller than bacteria, not larger. A cold is infectious: it is caused by a pathogen and spreads from person to person.

items.prompt:
Complete the description of how the body controls blood glucose (sugar).

After a large meal, the level of glucose in the blood {{0}}. The pancreas responds by releasing the hormone {{1}}, which signals body cells to take in glucose from the blood. As a result, blood glucose moves back toward its normal range. Because this response {{2}} the original change, it is an example of negative feedback.
items.hint: Digesting a meal adds sugar to the blood. Which pancreas hormone lowers blood sugar?
items.explain:
1. Digesting a meal releases glucose into the blood, so blood glucose rises.
  2. The pancreas releases insulin, which signals cells to take in glucose, lowering blood glucose. Glucagon is the hormone that does the opposite: it raises blood glucose when it is too low. Antibodies are immune proteins, not hormones.
  3. The response lowers glucose after it went up, so it reverses the change. Reversing a change is what makes a loop negative feedback; increasing the change would be positive feedback.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of negative feedback? Select three answers.
options: A person shivers when body temperature drops, and the heat produced warms the body.
During childbirth, contractions trigger the release of a hormone that causes even stronger contractions.
When the body is low on water, the kidneys make less urine, which helps conserve water.
At a cut, platelets release chemicals that attract more and more platelets until a clot forms.
When blood glucose drops too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, and blood glucose rises.
items.hint: For each one, ask: does the response push the condition back toward normal, or make the change bigger?
items.explain:
Negative feedback reverses a change:

  • Shivering: temperature falls → heat is produced → temperature rises back. Reverses the change.
  • Kidneys: water is low → less water is lost in urine → water levels are restored. Reverses the change.
  • Glucagon: glucose is low → glucagon causes glucose release → glucose rises back. Reverses the change.

Positive feedback makes a change bigger until an event ends it: childbirth contractions grow stronger until birth, and platelets attract more platelets until the clot forms. These two are the distractors.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Among these four volunteers, the one with the lowest resting heart rate was also the closest to his or her resting rate 3 minutes after jogging.
Jogging in place every day will permanently lower a person's resting heart rate.
Every volunteer's heart rate increased by the same number of beats per minute during jogging.
All adults return to their exact resting heart rate within 3 minutes after exercise.
items.hint: For each volunteer, subtract the resting rate from the 3-minutes-after rate. Then check whether each choice stays within what was measured.
items.explain:
Difference between 3 minutes after and resting:

  • A: 70 − 64 = 6
  • B: 80 − 72 = 8
  • C: 62 − 58 = 4
  • D: 76 − 70 = 6

Volunteer C has the lowest resting rate (58) and the smallest difference (4), so the first statement is supported for these four volunteers.

The study did not test daily jogging or long-term effects, so the "permanently lower" claim goes beyond the data. Increases during jogging were A: 64, B: 68, C: 58, D: 66, which are not the same. No volunteer was back to the exact resting rate after 3 minutes, and four volunteers cannot represent all adults.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: As the percent of vaccinated kindergarten children decreased, the reported cases per 100,000 people increased.
The vaccine caused the increase in cases of the disease.
The number of reported cases doubled every year from 2016 to 2020.
Any county with a vaccination rate below 90% will have more than 3 cases per 100,000 people.
items.hint: Describe the trend in each column. Then reject any answer that claims more than the table shows.
items.explain:
Reading the table: the vaccination rate fell every year (95 → 94 → 91 → 88 → 85%), and reported cases rose every year (0.4 → 0.5 → 1.2 → 3.8 → 9.6 per 100,000). So the first statement accurately describes the pattern. This pattern fits the idea of community immunity: when fewer people are immune, a contagious pathogen spreads more easily.

The vaccine could not have caused the increase, because cases rose as fewer children were vaccinated. Cases did not double every year: 0.4 to 0.5 is an increase of only 0.1. The last statement is about "any county," but the data come from one county only, so it goes beyond the data.
